# Hebrew (Biblical through Modern): Script, glyph change and Unicode

**Selection:** Middle Eastern language.  
**Lineage:** Afro-Asiatic → Semitic → West Semitic → Central Semitic → Northwest Semitic → Canaanite → Hebrew.

Hebrew script evolved from Phoenician-derived Paleo-Hebrew into the Aramaic-derived square script now used for Hebrew. The transition was gradual, not a one-time alphabet replacement; Paleo-Hebrew remained in some Second Temple settings. The consonantal alphabet has 22 core letters and five final-form variants for letters at word end. Matres lectionis provide some vowel cues, and Masoretic niqqud and cantillation marks were added later to represent a reading tradition. Modern prose is usually unpointed. Hebrew is written right-to-left; Unicode stores text in logical order and a bidi algorithm determines visual display.

The Hebrew block spans U+0590–U+05FF. Examples include bet ב U+05D1, final kaf ך U+05DA, sheva U+05B0, qamats U+05B8, dagesh U+05BC and shin dot U+05C1. Niqqud are combining points placed around a consonant; their position below a letter does not make them subscript letters. Fonts and traditions can vary in the visual placement and shape of points. Unicode code points do not store the stroke order, brush/pen movement or a manuscript allograph. Store Hebrew in logical RTL order, preserve marks when present, and test cursor, selection, punctuation and normalization behavior in mixed-direction text.

## Script and encoding inventory

| Sequence | Code points | Role / reading note |
|---|---|---|
| `ב` | `U+05D1` | bet |
| `ך` | `U+05DA` | final kaf, separate code point |
| `ְ` | `U+05B0` | sheva niqqud combining point |
| `ָ` | `U+05B8` | qamats niqqud combining point |
| `שׁ` | `U+05E9 + U+05C1` | shin with combining shin dot |

### Major writing-system stages

| Stage |
|---|
| Proto-Canaanite / Phoenician alphabet traditions |
| Paleo-Hebrew in Iron Age contexts |
| Gradual adoption of Aramaic-derived square script in Persian period |
| Masoretic niqqud and cantillation in manuscript reading traditions |
| Modern mostly unpointed Hebrew in RTL digital text |

**Normalization:** Keep logical RTL character order and combining marks. NFC/NFD may change code-point sequences; test mixed-direction punctuation and selection. Do not remove niqqud from pointed source text.

**Subscript status:** Niqqud can appear below a consonant but are combining vowel points, not subscript letters; Hebrew has no native subscript letters.

**Glyph / stroke note:** Paleo-Hebrew and square letters have distinct historical strokes and shapes. Vowel points are later combining signs around consonants; final forms are separate letters. Unicode encodes text and combining marks, not handwriting paths.

## Sources

# Mandarin Chinese (Standard Mandarin focus): Lineage, root age and sibling branches

**Selection:** Asian / Sinitic language.  
**Lineage:** Sino-Tibetan → Sinitic → Mandarin → Standard Mandarin.

**Root-age record:** Bayesian phylogenetic studies estimate initial Sino-Tibetan divergence at 5,871 BP and 7,184 BP in two 2019 studies; a broader 131-language study estimated a mean root age of 7,983 BP (95% highest posterior density interval 4,778–11,285 BP). BP uses the 1950 baseline. These modeled family ages are not dates for the Sinitic split, Old Chinese writing, or Mandarin. Late Shang oracle-bone records independently attest written Old Chinese in the 13th–11th centuries BCE.

**Evidence type:** Bayesian lexical phylogeny with historical calibrations; separate inscriptional attestation for Old Chinese. **Confidence:** moderate for an ancient family root; calendar estimates and top-level branching depend on sample, cognate coding, calibrations, and model.

**Dating limit:** The models support an ancestor older than 2,500–3,500 years, but they do not date Mandarin or the Sinitic branch directly. Sino-Tibetan internal classification and the Sinitic/non-Sinitic branching model remain debated. Oracle-bone writing dates an artifact record, not spoken language origin.

| Root-age audit field | Value |
|---|---|
| Requested minimum | 2500 years BP |
| Qualifying ancestor evidence | 4778 BP |
| Reported range | 4778–11285 BP |
| Ancestor stage | Sino-Tibetan family root (proposed phylogenetic root) |
| Assessment | meets threshold in published models; exact age and top-level branching are uncertain |

**Sibling branches / comparison set:** Jin (sometimes grouped with or near Mandarin); Wu; Gan; Xiang; Hakka; Yue; Min; Hui; Pinghua (inventories vary by classification); Tibetic (wider-family comparison); Burmese (wider-family comparison); Karenic (wider-family comparison); Lolo-Burmese and Himalayan languages (wider-family comparisons; subgroup relations are debated).

Mandarin is a Sinitic language in the Sino-Tibetan family. The Sinitic group includes Mandarin and other major branches commonly labeled Jin, Wu, Gan, Xiang, Hakka, Yue, Min, Hui and Pinghua, but subgroup boundaries and counts vary among scholars. Some classifications group Jin with Mandarin; others maintain it separately. These varieties are often called ‘Chinese dialects’ in non-linguistic contexts, but many are not mutually intelligible. Outside Sinitic, Sino-Tibetan includes Tibetic, Burmese, Karenic and many Himalayan languages; proposed higher-level relationships vary.

Three Bayesian lexical studies give different estimates for the first Sino-Tibetan divergence: 5,871 BP and 7,184 BP in two 2019 models, and a mean of 7,983 BP (95% highest posterior density 4,778–11,285 BP) in a broader 2020 sample of 131 languages. All place the family root well beyond 2,500–3,500 years, but these are model-based dates. They depend on which languages and cognates are sampled, the calibration strategy and tree model. They date a proposed root of Sino-Tibetan—not Mandarin, not the Sinitic split as a separately observed event, and not the first written Chinese. Top-level branching remains a debated research question.

Old Chinese refers to an early historical stage before the Qin unification, reconstructed through rhyme patterns, phonetic components in characters, later rhyme dictionaries, dialect evidence, loanwords and comparison. Oracle-bone texts from the Late Shang provide very early direct writing, but a written stage is not a dated proto-language root. Mandarin’s own history is much later: the 1324 Zhongyuan Yinyun is a key Old Mandarin rhyme book, while its phonological system appears to reflect features already established earlier in northern China. Classical written Chinese also had a long history across regions and cannot be equated with one spoken Mandarin lineage.

# Mandarin Chinese (Standard Mandarin focus): Chronology and evidence

**Selection:** Asian / Sinitic language.  
**Lineage:** Sino-Tibetan → Sinitic → Mandarin → Standard Mandarin.

The family-level root date and the writing timeline use different evidence. Bayesian models put the first Sino-Tibetan divergence at 5,871 BP, 7,184 BP and a 2020 mean of 7,983 BP (95% highest posterior density interval 4,778–11,285 BP), depending on dataset and method. These estimates are not inscriptions and do not directly date either Sinitic or Mandarin. The earliest known systematic Chinese writing appears in Late Shang oracle-bone inscriptions, with major corpora from roughly the thirteenth century BCE; these artifacts are a firm written anchor for Old Chinese, not a family split date. Middle Chinese is reconstructed from the Qieyun rhyme tradition beginning in 601 CE; the 1324 Zhongyuan Yinyun documents a system called Old Mandarin. The Cambridge historical phonology account stresses that the rhyme book’s system was composite and represents a prestigious northern standard rather than one village dialect.

Script history and speech history overlap but are not identical. Oracle-bone, bronze, seal, clerical, cursive, running and regular scripts are visual and material traditions; regional character forms and writing styles continued to coexist. On 28 January 1956, the PRC State Council approved a scheme for simplifying Chinese characters; the resolution records preceding public review and implementation. Pinyin was adopted by the PRC in 1958 as a Romanization scheme. Simplified character reform and standard-language policy are modern social/orthographic developments, not sound changes that produced Mandarin. Every time line in the data marks whether a date applies to a family model, an artifact, a rhyme tradition, a state policy or a reconstructed speech stage.

# Mandarin Chinese (Standard Mandarin focus): Sound changes and historical correspondences

**Selection:** Asian / Sinitic language.  
**Lineage:** Sino-Tibetan → Sinitic → Mandarin → Standard Mandarin.

Old Chinese phonology is reconstructed, not read directly off characters. Evidence comes from rhymes, shared phonetic components, Middle Chinese rhyme dictionaries and later dialects, with alternative reconstructions in the literature. Reconstructions generally posit contrasts and syllable shapes unlike modern Mandarin. Middle Chinese retained stop codas /-p, -t, -k/ in the entering-tone category; these codas were lost in Mandarin varieties, and the lexical items were distributed among later tone categories. The exact outcomes vary by initial class and Mandarin history. Across Sinitic branches, earlier onset voicing conditioned tone/register splits, but details differ by branch.

Modern Standard Mandarin has four lexical tones and a neutral tone, restricted syllable structures, and mainly nasal finals /n, ŋ/; historical stop codas are absent. Tone sandhi such as third-tone alternation is a synchronic phonological process and must not be confused with the historical origin of the tone system. Romanized Pinyin marks tones for learning and transcription, while Han characters are not alphabetic spellings of one segment at a time. The module records evidence type and period for each correspondence and does not pretend that modern pronunciations can be obtained by applying three simple sound laws to oracle-bone writing.

## Documented correspondences and scoped changes

| Change | Input / environment | Outcome | Example | Scope and limitation | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Loss of entering-tone stop codas in Mandarin | Middle Chinese syllables ending in /-p, -t, -k/ | stop codas disappear in Mandarin varieties; items redistribute among later tones | Middle Chinese “entering tone” category no longer exists as a final-stop category in Standard Mandarin | Historical outcomes depend on initial class, dialect and tone history; not a single tone mapping. | [M3](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/phonological-history-of-chinese/an-introduction-to-chinese-historical-phonology/7A1DECBDCB0C27F0486F3409A697D592), [M4](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/phonological-history-of-chinese/old-mandarin-the-zhongyuan-yinyun/25E3AB35BFBE15663813AA730A0F09EC) |
| Onset-voicing-conditioned tone/register splits | earlier voiced versus voiceless onset classes in historical Chinese | conditioned tonal/register distinctions in multiple Sinitic branches | historical tone categories do not map uniformly across Mandarin and non-Mandarin branches | Branch-specific; the short record stores the conditioning relation, not a complete tone correspondence table. | [M3](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/phonological-history-of-chinese/an-introduction-to-chinese-historical-phonology/7A1DECBDCB0C27F0486F3409A697D592), [M5](https://academic.oup.com/book/38951/chapter-abstract/338155819) |
| Old Mandarin rhyme-system reorganization | Middle Chinese distinctions in rhyme and tone categories | substantial reorganization documented in the 1324 Zhongyuan Yinyun system | the rhyme book describes Old Mandarin and shares core traits with Modern Mandarin | The book reflects a standard/composite phonological system and earlier northern innovations. | [M4](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/phonological-history-of-chinese/old-mandarin-the-zhongyuan-yinyun/25E3AB35BFBE15663813AA730A0F09EC) |

# Mandarin Chinese (Standard Mandarin focus): Syllable structure, prosody and sentence patterns

**Selection:** Asian / Sinitic language.  
**Lineage:** Sino-Tibetan → Sinitic → Mandarin → Standard Mandarin.

A broad Mandarin syllable template is often written (C)(G)V(X), where X includes restricted nasal finals and, in some analyses, an r-colored ending. The template is an approximation: consonant inventories, glide sequences, tone combinations, erhua and syllabic nasal analyses require more detail. A Chinese character generally corresponds to one syllable and a morpheme, while most spoken words contain one or more morphemes and many are disyllabic compounds. Character boundaries, morpheme boundaries and word boundaries are therefore not interchangeable.

Standard Mandarin clauses commonly use subject–verb–object order and topic–comment organization. Aspect particles, coverbs, classifiers, resultative complements and word order carry much grammatical information; the language has little inflectional morphology compared with Latin or Hebrew. Spoken varieties differ, and written Classical Chinese is not the grammar of modern conversation. The profile gives a broad standard-Mandarin view with a source-backed reminder that “Chinese” covers multiple spoken Sinitic systems. Sentence parsing should include topic and aspect rather than reading word order as the only grammatical cue.

## Compact structural record

| Feature | Summary |
|---|---|
| Syllable profile | Approximate modern Standard Mandarin pattern (C)(G)V(X), restricted nasal endings, lexical tones plus neutral tone; historical Old Chinese was different. |
| Sentence pattern | Standard Mandarin is broadly SVO and topic-comment; aspect particles, classifiers, coverbs and complements are central. |

# Mandarin Chinese (Standard Mandarin focus): Script, glyph change and Unicode

**Selection:** Asian / Sinitic language.  
**Lineage:** Sino-Tibetan → Sinitic → Mandarin → Standard Mandarin.

Chinese writing has continuous use across more than three millennia, with major material and calligraphic forms including oracle-bone, bronze, seal, clerical, cursive, running and regular script. Early incised characters often have angular strokes suited to bone or metal; seal forms favor balanced, even lines; clerical writing develops prominent horizontal and descending strokes; brush-based cursive can omit or join strokes. These are histories of glyph shape and writing technique, not a single standardized stroke order for every historical object. Modern Unicode Han characters encode unified abstract ideographs; a font selects a glyph form, and regional variants can differ visibly.

The main CJK Unified Ideographs block is U+4E00–U+9FFF, with additional extension blocks; a code point such as 好 U+597D is not itself a pronunciation or a stroke-order recipe. Simplified and traditional forms coexist. Pinyin tone vowels may use precomposed letters such as ā U+0101, ǎ U+01CE and ǚ U+01DA, or base vowels plus combining marks U+0304, U+0301, U+030C and U+0300; ü is U+00FC. Pinyin is an auxiliary alphabetic system. Han script has no native subscript letters. Unicode NFC/NFD handles equivalent encoded sequences, not tone interpretation or calligraphic strokes.

| `̄` | `U+0304` | combining macron, first tone |
| `ǔ` | `U+0075 + U+030C` | decomposed u plus combining caron; diaeresis may add U+0308 |

### Major writing-system stages

| Stage |
|---|
| Oracle-bone inscriptions |
| Bronze inscriptions and regional Warring States forms |
| Qin small seal and Han clerical forms |
| Regular, running and cursive calligraphy |
| 1956 PRC character-simplification scheme and later standards |
| Modern traditional/simplified forms and Unicode encoding |

**Normalization:** Preserve Pinyin tone and ü distinctions. Use NFC/NFD consistently for text matching; do not strip tone marks or treat a Han character code point as its pronunciation.

**Subscript status:** No native subscript letters in Mandarin Han writing or Hanyu Pinyin. Linguistic reconstruction notation is separate.

**Glyph / stroke note:** Incision, seal cutting and brush movement produce different visible strokes. Running and cursive can join or omit strokes. The 1956 reform codified a set of simplified forms; later standards and regional practice affect which forms are in use. Unicode encodes characters, not the physical stroke sequence; glyph forms vary by font and region.

The requested comparison floor is 2,500 years. | Selected language | Ancestor or family stage | Age evidence used | Comparison relatives | Limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Spanish | Archaic Latin / early Italic record | Seventh–sixth century BCE inscriptions, about 2,550–2,650 BP [S1](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/indoeuropean-language-family/italic/473A395FABB6E9FB91AE75076F390D29) | Portuguese, Galician, Astur-Leonese, Aragonese, and wider Romance descendants | Artifact dates anchor Latin writing, not Spanish birth |
| Fijian | Proto-Oceanic | About 3,000–3,300 BP; archaeology-informed family dating [F2](https://press.anu.edu.au/downloads/press/p69411/mobile/ch03.html), [F3](https://doi.org/10.1093/jole/lzz009) | Related Fijian varieties and Polynesian through Central Pacific history | Reconstructed ancestor and calibration, not written attestation |
| Mandarin | Sino-Tibetan family root | Bayesian model means 5,871, 7,184 and 7,983 BP; 2020 95% HPD 4,778–11,285 BP [M11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-77404-4), [M12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1153-z), [M13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6534992/) | Sinitic branches and wider Tibetic, Burmese, Karenic and Himalayan comparisons | This estimates the wider family root, not the Sinitic split or Mandarin; model/sample/topology vary |
| Yoruba | Niger-Congo macrofamily expansion estimate; local Yoruboid stage separate | A Cambridge overview and a Language Science Press volume place Niger-Congo expansion or macrofamily depth near or above 12,000 BP, while stressing unresolved deep classification [Y3](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/42051/chapter/355823946), [Y13](https://doi.org/10.1017/9781107279872.018), [Y14](https://langsci-press.org/catalog/view/190/1074/1266-2) | Igala, Itsekiri, and Yoruba varieties | Broad expansion estimate is not a securely reconstructed Proto-Niger-Congo date; local model spans about 2,300–4,500 BP [Y1](https://iupress.org/9780253051486/the-yoruba/), [Y2](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/yoruba-from-prehistory-to-the-present/geography-and-society/CC682B3D24A7A9648C018BABC1E2EDEA) |
| Hebrew | Canaanite within Northwest Semitic | Canaanite evidence c.1550–1200 BCE, about 3,150–3,500 BP [H1](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/ancient-languages-of-syriapalestine-and-arabia/hebrew/512F0FC4796BF3DB1137C1A9BA228DB1), [H2](https://sites.utexas.edu/scripts/files/2020/10/2019-AWW-The-Canaanite-Languages.pdf) | Phoenician, Ammonite, Moabite, Edomite; Aramaic as a close relative | Hebrew differentiation is gradual; the evidence dates Canaanite and early Hebrew features, not Modern Hebrew |

## Programmatic check

Every profile’s `rootEvidence.ageAssessment` stores the requested floor, a qualifying age claim, any numeric range, ancestor-stage label, qualification note and source keys. The JavaScript helper `auditRootAgeCriteria(profiles)` checks that each estimate reaches 2,500 BP, each root assessment cites registered profile sources, and each profile has at least three comparison entries. It reports uncertainty text verbatim instead of converting model estimates into an objective date. Run it directly with `node Onyx/js/language-history/research/run-invariants.js` or import it from the shared research index.

## Interpretation

The age audit is a traceability check, not a statistical reanalysis. Mandarin’s wider confidence interval and competing trees remain visible. Yoruba’s macrofamily estimate is expressly qualified because Niger-Congo’s deepest structure and reconstruction are unsettled. The audit checks whether each entry gives a sourced claim above the floor; it does not certify that competing models are equally strong.

# Spanish: Lineage, root age and sibling branches

**Selection:** Romance language.  
**Lineage:** Indo-European → Italic → Latin → Romance → Ibero-Romance → Castilian / Spanish.

**Root-age record:** Latin inscriptions survive from the seventh–sixth centuries BCE; some individual early inscriptions have contested dating or language attribution.

**Evidence type:** inscriptional attestation. **Confidence:** high for attestation; moderate for individual object dating.

**Dating limit:** This is the age of an ancestor and written record, not the birth date of Spanish. Spoken Latin diversified regionally over centuries; Spanish is a medieval Romance language.

| Root-age audit field | Value |
|---|---|
| Requested minimum | 2500 years BP |
| Qualifying ancestor evidence | 2549 BP |
| Reported range | 2549–2649 BP |
| Ancestor stage | Archaic Latin inscriptional record |
| Assessment | meets threshold at the early Romance ancestor level |

**Sibling branches / comparison set:** Portuguese and Galician; Astur-Leonese; Aragonese; Catalan (its position within Romance classifications is described differently); French; Italian; Sardinian; Romanian.

Spanish belongs to Romance, the descendant group of Latin, within Indo-European. A useful working path is Indo-European → Italic → Latin → Romance → Ibero-Romance → Castilian/Spanish. These labels describe different levels: Latin is an attested language; Proto-Italic and Proto-Indo-European are reconstructed ancestors; Romance is a family of daughter languages, not a single uniform stage. Roman Latin is documented in archaic inscriptions by the seventh–sixth centuries BCE, while the familiar medieval and modern forms of Spanish arose much later. The Roman expansion spread Latin across regions whose speech later developed into multiple Romance languages.

Spanish has close comparisons with Portuguese and Galician and broader Romance comparisons with Astur-Leonese, Aragonese, Catalan, French, Italian, Sardinian and Romanian. The exact grouping and status of some varieties varies among classification traditions. Shared descent is established through recurring sound correspondences and inherited morphology, not simply shared vocabulary or present-day mutual understanding. Contact, learned Latin vocabulary and later standardization complicate every branch boundary. This profile treats the tree as a useful model and records where classification is not uniform.

# Spanish: Chronology and evidence

**Selection:** Romance language.  
**Lineage:** Indo-European → Italic → Latin → Romance → Ibero-Romance → Castilian / Spanish.

The chronology distinguishes dated writing from reconstructed speech. Early Latin inscriptions from the seventh–sixth centuries BCE are the firmest anchor; the exact age and interpretation of individual objects can be debated. Latin later gains more epigraphic and literary documentation. During the first millennium CE, regional spoken Latin changes and differentiates; there is no single day when Latin ‘became’ Spanish. Medieval Iberian records show early Romance varieties and Castilian written practice. The 1492 grammar by Antonio de Nebrija is a milestone in codification, while printing, administration, colonial expansion and later academy work spread and standardize particular forms. None of these is a family split date.

Spanish spelling records historical layers unevenly. Some inherited sound changes are reflected in spelling, others were later regularized, and learned words often retain forms closer to Latin than inherited everyday words. The code therefore stores chronology rows with an evidence label: inscription, literary record, orthographic milestone, or reconstruction. A reconstructed stage should never be presented as an artifact date, and a modern standard should not be projected unchanged into medieval speech.

## Dated milestones and evidence

| 1st millennium CE | Regional spoken Latin differentiates into Romance varieties over centuries | comparative reconstruction and written record | high for gradual diversification; no single split year | [S2](https://academic.oup.com/book/26021) |
| Medieval period | Early Romance and Castilian writing becomes visible in surviving records | manuscript attestation | high as a broad period | [S2](https://academic.oup.com/book/26021), [S6](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/latin-palaeography/latin-script-in-antiquity/7AAE013BCD262AB689DE4B2FAAD02B0D) |

# Spanish: Sound changes and historical correspondences

**Selection:** Romance language.  
**Lineage:** Indo-European → Italic → Latin → Romance → Ibero-Romance → Castilian / Spanish.

Several characteristic Castilian developments can be compared with Latin while remaining explicitly conditioned. Stressed Latin short-mid vowels often diphthongized: compare terra with tierra and porta with puerta. This pattern is associated with stressed syllables and has lexical and historical exceptions; it is not a rule that converts every written e or o. In parts of northern Iberian Romance, Latin word-initial /f/ before a vowel passed through an aspirated stage commonly written h and later lost its aspiration in much of standard Spanish: farina → medieval harina → modern silent h, and filium → hijo. /f/ remains in many consonant clusters, learned words and later borrowings, so the spelling h is not a live sound rule.

Latin voiceless stops between vowels often became voiced in inherited Spanish words, as in vita → vida; in contemporary Spanish the voiced stop phonemes commonly have approximant realizations in these positions. Latin case inflection also weakened across the transition to Romance, with prepositions, clitics and constituent order carrying more grammatical work. These are broad historical tendencies, not a universal derivation engine. Dialect, chronology, analogy and lexical history explain exceptions. The JavaScript rules are evidence records with scope notes, not code that rewrites arbitrary Latin words.

## Documented correspondences and scoped changes

| Change | Input / environment | Outcome | Example | Scope and limitation | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stressed-vowel diphthongization | Latin stressed short /ɛ, ɔ/ in inherited lexical items | often /je, we/ in Spanish | terra → tierra; porta → puerta | Conditioned by stress and historical/lexical environment; exceptions exist. | [S2](https://academic.oup.com/book/26021), [S3](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/cambridge-handbook-of-spanish-linguistics/syllable/CB48DEE6ECF4EAD91E816486BA8E8573) |
| Initial Latin f weakening | Latin word-initial /f/ before a vowel in relevant Castilian inherited words | medieval aspiration written h, later usually zero in standard Spanish | farina → harina; filium → hijo | Regional and lexical; clusters, learned forms and later loans often retain f. | [S2](https://academic.oup.com/book/26021), [S8](https://revistas.ucm.es/index.php/RFRM/es/article/view/71878) |
| Intervocalic stop voicing / lenition | inherited Latin voiceless stops between vowels | often voiced; voiced stops are commonly approximants in modern Spanish environments | vita → vida | Not all tokens are inherited or regular in the same way; phonetic realization varies. | [S2](https://academic.oup.com/book/26021) |

# Spanish: Syllable structure, prosody and sentence patterns

**Selection:** Romance language.  
**Lineage:** Indo-European → Italic → Latin → Romance → Ibero-Romance → Castilian / Spanish.

A practical broad Spanish syllable template is (C)(C)V(C), with onset and coda restrictions shaped by sonority, dialect, word history and loan adaptation. Spanish has five oral vowel phonemes. Vowel sequences may form diphthongs or triphthongs, or hiatus; written accent rules do not simply mirror every speaker’s phonetic syllabification. Default lexical stress is predictable from the final letter, and an acute accent marks stress when spelling rules require it, as well as some grammatical distinctions. The RAE’s orthographic rules treat specified vowel sequences consistently for accentuation even where phonetic realization may vary.

Unmarked declaratives commonly follow subject–verb–object order, but Spanish permits flexible order for discourse focus and often omits a recoverable subject pronoun. Verb agreement, clitics, prepositions and information structure interact with word order. A sentence diagram for Spanish therefore needs to record both a neutral order and pragmatic alternatives; it should not infer a single fixed order from a short example. The profile lists broad patterns and directs detailed parsing to a grammar rather than pretending that a compact syllable expression or one SVO label captures every construction.

## Compact structural record

| Feature | Summary |
|---|---|
| Syllable profile | Broad template (C)(C)V(C); five oral vowels; stress and vowel sequence analysis are orthography- and dialect-sensitive. |
| Sentence pattern | Neutral SVO is common; flexible constituent order, null subjects, verb agreement, clitics and focus are central. |

# Spanish: Script, glyph change and Unicode

**Selection:** Romance language.  
**Lineage:** Indo-European → Italic → Latin → Romance → Ibero-Romance → Castilian / Spanish.

Spanish uses the Latin alphabet, whose Roman forms developed through earlier Greek and Etruscan writing traditions and later changed through monumental capitals, cursive hands, medieval book scripts, printing and modern type. These are changes in glyph design and writing practice; Unicode encodes abstract text characters, not the pen path, pressure, stroke order or historical allograph. In medieval manuscripts, a small superscript n used as an abbreviation for a doubled n contributed to the development of ñ. Modern Spanish treats ñ as a separate alphabet letter, whereas ch and ll are digraphs. Acute accents mark stress or contrasts according to spelling rules; ü indicates that u is pronounced in güe/güi. The inverted question and exclamation marks are punctuation.

Useful encodings include ñ U+00F1 (or n U+006E plus U+0303 in decomposed text), á U+00E1, ü U+00FC, ¿ U+00BF and ¡ U+00A1. NFC may store common accented letters as precomposed code points; NFD may represent them with a base letter and combining mark. Both can render the same grapheme. Spanish has no native subscript letters. A diaeresis, acute accent and tilde are not interchangeable marks: their linguistic function depends on the orthography, even where Unicode uses shared combining characters.

## Script and encoding inventory

| Sequence | Code points | Role / reading note |
|---|---|---|
| `ñ` | `U+00F1` | Spanish letter eñe; NFC example |
| `ñ` | `U+006E + U+0303` | NFD sequence rendering the same grapheme |
| `á` | `U+00E1` | acute-accented a |
| `é` | `U+00E9` | acute-accented e |
| `í` | `U+00ED` | acute-accented i |
| `ó` | `U+00F3` | acute-accented o |
| `ú` | `U+00FA` | acute-accented u |
| `ü` | `U+00FC` | u with diaeresis in güe/güi |
| `¿` | `U+00BF` | inverted question mark |
| `¡` | `U+00A1` | inverted exclamation mark |
| `́` | `U+0301` | combining acute accent in decomposed text |
| `̃` | `U+0303` | combining tilde in decomposed ñ |

### Major writing-system stages

| Stage |
|---|
| Roman capitals and cursive traditions |
| Late antique and medieval book/cursive scripts |
| Printing and early modern codification |
| Modern Spanish alphabet and punctuation |

**Normalization:** Preserve accents, ñ, ü and punctuation. Normalize at a system boundary, usually NFC for storage/display interoperability; never strip marks from canonical text.

**Subscript status:** No native subscript letters in the standard orthography. Linguistic subscripts in IPA or metadata belong to a separate notation layer.

**Glyph / stroke note:** Letterforms and writing tools change the visible stroke shape; the ñ tilde descends from an abbreviation mark over n in medieval practice. Unicode stores text values, not handwriting trajectories.

# Unicode, diacritics, glyphs and strokes

Unicode encodes abstract characters and combining marks. A user-perceived grapheme can consist of several code points: Spanish `n` + COMBINING TILDE can render as `ñ`; Yoruba `e` + DOT BELOW + ACUTE can render as `ẹ́`; Hebrew vowel points combine with a consonant; Pinyin can use precomposed tone vowels or decomposed base-plus-mark sequences. Unicode’s FAQ distinguishes a code point from an end-user grapheme and explains that a combining mark’s linguistic function is language-specific.

## Normalization

NFC and NFD are canonical representations of equivalent text. They can have different code-point sequences. The JavaScript utility reports code points before and after normalization; it does not remove accents or decide whether a spelling is correct. Normalize at system boundaries and preserve the source form when doing philological work. A 2026 Yorùbá speech-corpus preprint reports normalization inconsistencies in over 60% of its 24,905 sentence lines. That is a corpus-preparation result, not a measured rate for all Yorùbá digital text; it illustrates why tone and underdot sequences need explicit testing.

The same year, a preprint proposed using caron and circumflex for certain Yorùbá contour tones. These are existing Unicode marks, but the proposal does not make them part of standard Yorùbá spelling. Data pipelines should preserve the marks and attach orthographic status as metadata instead of silently rewriting text.

## Below-base marks and subscripts

Yoruba underdots and Hebrew niqqud may appear below a base letter, but they are combining diacritics or points, not subscript letters. The standard orthographies in this set have no native subscript letters. Linguists use subscript-like notation in IPA, phonetic narrow transcription or reconstructed notation; keep that in a separate annotation layer.

## Strokes and historical glyphs

The Chinese writing-system notes describe changes in material and brush practice: incision on bone, bronze inscription, seal forms, clerical brush strokes, and running/cursive joining or omission. Latin and Hebrew notes compare major script traditions and changing letter shapes. Fijian and Yoruba show how existing Latin glyphs gained language-specific values and marks. No Unicode string stores the historical pen path, order, pressure, carving motion or allograph. To preserve stroke-level history, a project needs separate paleographic image/vector data with provenance.
